generalizedRange: Southeast Asia, from Myanmar through Malaysia and Singapore to Sumatra, Java and Borneo
hook: No teeth, scales of fingernail, and the most trafficked mammals alive.

story.text: The Sunda pangolin is the only kind of mammal armoured head to tail in scales — keratin, the stuff of fingernails, grown from compressed hair.
It has no teeth; a sticky tongue does the work, taking in some two hundred thousand ants and termites a day.
Threatened, it curls into a ball with its soft belly inside and waits.
More climber than its Chinese cousin, it grips branches with a prehensile tail and dens in tree hollows.
One young is born after six or seven months and rides on its mother's back or tail.
In Asia it is the mammal most often found in illegal trade; the equivalent of more than 895,000 pangolins were trafficked worldwide from 2000 to 2019.
In September 2016 the nations of CITES voted all eight pangolin species onto Appendix I, closing international commercial trade.
At Cuc Phuong, Save Vietnam's Wildlife has taken in 1,823 pangolins from confiscations and returned 1,019 to the forest.
In Singapore, where roads are the greater danger, about a hundred still move through the island's reserves, and some twenty rescued each year pass through Mandai's hospital before release.
To witness the Sunda pangolin is to keep company with an animal whose only defence is to close — and to stand with those carrying it back to the trees.

reproduction.text: One young, rarely two, is born after a gestation of six to seven months, usually in a tree hollow; it rides on its mother's back or tail and stays with her for three or four months.

insight.text: A pangolin has no teeth and a tongue that reaches 25 cm — enough to take in roughly 200,000 ants and termites a day, or about 70 million in a year.

programs.title: Pangolin rescue, rehabilitation & release
programs.summary: Receives pangolins confiscated from traffickers at its Cuc Phuong centre, treats and rehabilitates them, and has returned 1,019 of 1,823 rescued pangolins to the wild with post-release monitoring.

programs.title: Singapore pangolin rescue & research
programs.summary: Treats the twenty-odd wild pangolins rescued in Singapore each year for release by NParks, radio-tracks animals to learn their ranges and road crossings, and co-chairs the Singapore Pangolin Working Group behind the 2018 national action plan.
